title: The h-Index

concept.title: Sort, then compare rank with value
body: A researcher has an **h-index** of `h` if `h` of their papers were cited at least `h` times each. Sort the citation counts in increasing order. The paper at position `i` (counting from 0) has `n - i` papers with at least its citations, itself included. So paper `i` supports an h-index of `min(c[i], n - i)`.

body.code:
c.sort()
h = 0
for i in range(n):
    h = max(h, min(c[i], n - i))

body: The answer is the largest such value. Sorting turns "how many papers have at least this many citations" into a simple position, a trick that is useful whenever a question compares a value with the number of elements above it.

statement: Given the number of citations of each of `n` papers, find the largest `h` such that at least `h` papers have at least `h` citations each.
inputFormat: The second line has `n` non-negative integers.

examples.note: Three papers (3, 6, 5) have at least 3 citations, but not four papers with 4. So h = 3.

hints: Sort the numbers in increasing order.
The paper at index i has `n - i` papers with at least as many citations (counting itself).
Take the maximum of `min(c[i], n - i)` over all i.

input = sys.stdin.readline

n = int(input())
c = list(map(int, input().split()))

explanation: After sorting increasingly, the paper at index `i` has `n - i` papers with at least its citations, so it supports an h-index of `min(c[i], n - i)`. The best of these is the answer.
solution.complexity: Time O(n log n), space O(1) besides sorting.

code.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

n = int(input())
c = list(map(int, input().split()))

c.sort()
h = 0
for i in range(n):
    h = max(h, min(c[i], n - i))
print(h)
